newsitem.title: USA: Airlines may see little change from Boeing merger.
newsitem.headline: Airlines may see little change from Boeing merger.

text.p: A merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp would have little impact on commercial aircraft prices, analysts said.
"I don't really expect there to be a change in pricing," said Susan Donofrio, an airline analyst with NatWest Securities Corp.
McDonnell Douglas has been a distant third behind Boeing and Airbus Industrie in landing new jet orders. It controls less than 10 percent of the U.S. commerical aircraft market, analysts said.

"If you were taking out a viable third party, the airlines would be worried. But as it is now, McDonnell Douglas's share of new orders has declined precipitously in recent years," said Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber.
Removing McDonnell Douglas from the commercial aircraft market will not have a "pervasive effect" on pricing or airlines' acquisition strategies, Buttrick said.
"Airbus and Boeing have demonstrated that a duopoly can be effective," he said.
The proposed Boeing-McDonnell deal may put pressure on Airbus to restructure, analysts said.
Airbus is a consortium made up of French state-owned Ste Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz's aerospace unit, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA of Spain.
Talks on changing the current Airbus partnership into an integrated company that would rival an expanded Boeing have gone slowly.
An expanded Boeing would force Airbus to fight harder to attain its goal of controlling 50 percent of the worldwide civilian aircraft market by the end of the decade, analysts said.
Historically, Airbus has held about 30 percent of the market, behind Boeing's 60 percent.
A more competitive Airbus would benefit airlines analysts said.
"Maybe two (manufacturers) is enough competition for the airlines." Don Baker, a former U.S. antitrust official, said in an interview on CNBC.
Most U.S. airlines declined comment on the proposed Boeing-McDonnell deal, saying it was too early to predict whether the merger would affect aircraft pricing.
It's like looking into a crystal ball to tell what would be coming down the pipeline," said Delta Air Lines Inc spokesman Tod Clay.
